# Synthetic educational etch overview

> This is a synthetic educational document created for the FabSight simulation. It > is not a real production SOP.

Etching is a broad semiconductor fabrication stage that selectively removes material from exposed regions of a wafer. Earlier patterning steps define which regions should be affected. Educational process-control discussions often consider uniformity, selectivity, pattern transfer, repeatability, and inspection feedback. These concepts describe general engineering goals rather than a detailed recipe.

An investigation of unusual etch results may compare current observations with historical baselines, review equipment alarms and maintenance context, check whether the observation is isolated or recurring, and examine inspection patterns. A wafer edge abnormality may motivate review of edge handling, uniformity, masking, and inspection behavior as possible areas to investigate. Cleaning, deposition, lithography, implantation, chemical mechanical planarization, and inspection interact as conceptual stages in a manufacturing route. Evidence from one stage should be interpreted with timestamps, measurement quality, and provenance.

# Synthetic educational process-monitoring guide

> This is a synthetic educational document created for the FabSight simulation. It > is not a real production SOP.

Process monitoring compares manufacturing observations with expected behavior. Basic statistical process control concepts include a stable baseline, natural variation, special-cause signals, control charts, and careful review of data quality. A control signal is evidence for investigation; it is not by itself proof of a defect cause.

For deposition, lithography, etch, implantation, cleaning, and CMP, useful educational questions include whether a change is persistent, whether multiple measurements move together, whether the event timing aligns with maintenance or alarms, and whether an inspection result repeats across lots. Anonymous variables should retain anonymous names unless authoritative source metadata defines their physical meanings.

Equipment maintenance context can help organize an investigation. Preventive work, calibration checks, inspections, and generic alarms should be reviewed chronologically. Correlation between an alarm and a quality observation does not establish causality. A structured investigation records competing explanations, conflicting evidence, missing information, and the provenance of every reference.

Anomaly investigation begins with verification: confirm the sample identity, inspect missing values, compare against a suitable baseline, and check whether the observation is reproducible. Quality engineering favors traceable evidence over unsupported conclusions.

# Synthetic educational wafer-inspection notes

> This is a synthetic educational document created for the FabSight simulation. It > is not a real production SOP.

A wafer map is a spatial grid of die-level inspection or test states, not an ordinary photograph. Groups of abnormal dies can form patterns such as center, donut, edge-local, edge-ring, local, random, scratch, near-full, or none. Pattern names describe geometry and do not reveal a physical root cause.

An edge-ring pattern concentrates abnormal die states around much of the wafer edge. An edge-local pattern is more confined to part of the perimeter. A scratch pattern is often visually linear, while a random pattern is more dispersed. Classification confidence describes model output, not certainty that a production mechanism is known.

When process risk and visual evidence disagree, the conflict should be preserved for investigation rather than automatically resolved.
